Depuis quelques mois, les vaccins contre: For the past few months, COVID-19 vaccines have been on everyone’s lips in Quebec. Health authorities keep hammering home that mass vaccination is the only way to put an end to the pandemic. But is it accessible to everyone?
‍Il est 12 h 30, mardi après-midi, et Ro: It’s 12:30 p.m. on a Tuesday afternoon, and Rose Ngo Ndjel is running in every direction. The line of people waiting for the food distribution is growing longer in front of the William-Hingston Centre in Parc-Extension. “We have to wait because the truck broke down!” shouts Ms. Ngo Ndjel, director of the organization Afrique au Féminin. Every week, she oversees the food distribution in the neighbourhood.
D’une voix dynamique, elle répète tout e: In an energetic voice, she repeats everything in English. Community workers from the local neighbourhood roundtable pass the word along in Hindi, Punjabi and Greek. The crowd waits patiently; children play and seniors catch up with their neighbours while roundtable members hand out masks. The line, about a hundred people long, reflects the diversity of the neighbourhood.
Certains, qui sont demandeurs d’asile, s: Some are asylum seekers who arrived in Montréal in recent months; others were born in the city. For the past few weeks, there have also been some new faces. Two social workers from the local CLSC are promoting vaccination in several languages with the help of young interpreters from the neighbourhood roundtable. They answer residents’ many questions:
« Oui, toute personne âgée de 18 ans et: “Yes, anyone 18 and older is eligible now. There will be a nurse who can talk to you about side effects,” says one of them. “No, you don’t need a health insurance card. Vaccination is for everyone,” answers the other.
Une file d’attente se forme devant le ce: A line forms in front of the William-Hingston Centre in Parc-Extension.
« Au début de la crise, il y avait vraim: “At the start of the crisis, there were really a lot of barriers to testing and care for undocumented people,” explains Jill Hanley, co-founder of the Immigrant Workers Centre (IWC), a Montréal organization that defends the rights of immigrant workers.
« J’ai été agréablement surprise de voir: “I was pleasantly surprised to see how quickly action was taken to make testing, COVID-related care and vaccination free for everyone.”
Elle ajoute que le niveau de collaborati: She adds that the level of collaboration she sees between health authorities and the community sector is indeed unprecedented: “We haven’t worked this closely together in the past, because before the pandemic, the need wasn’t the same!”
Le Canada est souvent primé pour les soi: Canada is often praised for its so-called universal health care. In practice, however, that care is covered only for people who hold a Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) card.
Les personnes sans statut, les demandeur: People without status, asylum seekers, people who arrived in the country less than three months ago, international students and many temporary workers do not have this privilege. Across Canada, more than a million people are not entitled to a health insurance card or are at risk of losing it, according to the <l1>Migrant Rights Network</l1>, a pan-Canadian network of migrant worker rights organizations that is calling for permanent resident status for all.
La pandémie, toutefois, a amélioré l’acc: The pandemic, however, has improved access to health care for people with precarious status. In Ontario, health care has been free for everyone for the past year. In Quebec, the expansion of access is more modest, but testing, COVID-19-related health care and vaccination are indeed free for everyone.
« La vaccination est offerte à tous, san: “Vaccination is offered to everyone, free of charge and regardless of status, both for vaccines included in the Quebec immunization program and for vaccines offered as part of special vaccination campaigns, as is the case for COVID-19,” says the Ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux.
« Une personne qui n’a pas de carte d’as: “A person who doesn’t have a health insurance card can indeed get vaccinated,” says Noémie Vanheuverzwijn, spokesperson for the Ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux. She says people must provide their date of birth, but are under no obligation to prove it with identification.
« L’objectif de la campagne de vaccinati: “The goal of the vaccination campaign is to vaccinate as many Quebecers as possible in order to reduce the incidence of COVID-19,” says Ms. Vanheuverzwijn. That is, in her words, why the vaccination campaign must not exclude people without a health insurance card. She adds that the information provided at a vaccination centre is in no way shared with the federal government.
« J’ai entendu dire qu’il faut avoir une: “I heard you need proof of age, but I can surely show my passport or something,” says Mamadou, who doesn’t have a health insurance card. The Guinean asylum seeker, who works in construction, wants to get vaccinated. It’s thanks to IWC community workers that he now knows the steps to follow. He hasn’t booked an appointment yet.
Bien que la vaccination soit offerte à t: Although vaccination is open to everyone, people without a health insurance card face several barriers. Of 12 pharmacies in Greater Montréal offering COVID-19 vaccination that were contacted at random, only 3 said it was not necessary to show identification. Three others required some form of ID, and three said they did not know how to proceed. One pharmacy asked for a social insurance number.
Enfin, dans deux pharmacies, il n’a pas: Finally, at two pharmacies, it was not possible to speak directly to anyone. “The problem that remains is that people have to identify themselves,” notes Pénélope Boudreault, national director of Médecins du Monde Canada (MDM), based in Montréal. She explains that even when they have identification, many people are afraid to identify themselves because of their status.
« Dans les centres de vaccination de mas: “In the mass vaccination centres, there are still gaps in the protocol – employees will ask for the RAMQ card or simply ask a lot of questions, which risks scaring people away.” She says she has received calls from people who were refused access to vaccination, but specifies that these are rarer than the cases of people being refused testing at the start of the pandemic.
Pour aider à répondre au problème, Médec: To help address the problem, Médecins du Monde and CoVivre, an emergency response program, are producing proof-of-identity documents specifically for vaccination. “Despite our efforts, I can’t guarantee 100% that these documents will work,” laments Pénélope Boudreault.
Une solution potentielle est la mise sur: One potential solution is setting up temporary walk-in pop-up clinics organized by local CLSCs and community organizations. People can get vaccinated there in a safe, accessible environment. According to several community workers, these clinics are more appealing than mass vaccination centres for vulnerable clients.
« Au début de la vaccination, on m’a inv: “At the beginning of the vaccination campaign, I was invited to visit a mass vaccination centre on the Université de Montréal’s MIL campus. The Parc-Extension community wasn’t there,” laments Rose Ngo Ndjel. “These are people who walk, and when it’s too far, they don’t go,” the community worker explains. “But when the CLSC organized a pop-up clinic here, every single dose was snapped up,” she says, so much so that in the line in front of the William-Hingston Centre that Tuesday morning, about three-quarters of the adults had already been vaccinated.
Ousseynou Ndiaye est directeur de l’orga: Ousseynou Ndiaye is director of the organization Un itinéraire pour tous, in Montréal-Nord. He stresses the need for local vaccination centres, with the participation of community workers. He believes that setting up accessible pop-up clinics, combined with the efforts of community sector workers who reach out to residents and welcome them at vaccination sites, should “pay off” in the long term. “Pop-up clinics are effective, because we take the time to talk to everyone,” he continues.
C’est exigeant, mais ça marche. Nous app: “It’s demanding, but it works. We call everyone, we send WhatsApp messages; we reassure them, we even have volunteers who can drive people to the centres.” Once there, participants are supported by community workers who know them and speak their language. Mr. Ndiaye reiterates that there is no police presence near these clinics.
« On informe les autorités quand on orga: “We inform the authorities when we organize an event, but on site, it’s only us, the borough staff and the vaccinators,” he says. “Nobody’s going to ask you for your papers.”
La clinique de vaccination sans rendez-v: The walk-in vaccination clinic in Parc-Extension generated enthusiasm among people in the neighbourhood.
M. Ndiaye et ses collaborateurs ont pass: Mr. Ndiaye and his colleagues have spent long hours on the phone persuading neighbourhood residents to come to a pop-up clinic. A recent survey conducted by the organization found that only 37% of respondents said they would get vaccinated as soon as possible. Most of those who were hesitant wanted to see what effects vaccination had on others before getting a vaccine themselves. “We don’t sense a lot of enthusiasm for vaccination. Many people don’t trust vaccines,” Mr. Ndiaye acknowledges.
Sur 63 appels effectués, à peine 5 inter: Of 63 calls made, barely 5 people told him they would get vaccinated. In his view, the distrust is partly due to the pharmaceutical companies themselves, which have carried out sometimes dubious clinical trials in several countries in Africa and the Caribbean. In the spring of 2020, the bungling around a COVID-19 testing site in Montréal-Nord, dismantled just a few days later on the pretext that it was a study, did nothing to correct this feeling. The revelations about the rare cases of blood clots linked to the AstraZeneca vaccine were also a blow. “People say they don’t want to be guinea pigs,” Mr. Ndiaye sums up.
Il appelle les autorités à faire davanta: He is calling on the authorities to do more outreach in the neighbourhood’s churches and mosques, and to understand that earning anyone’s trust takes time. Some migrant workers, however, hesitate to get vaccinated for other reasons. Jill Hanley, of the IWC, now hardly receives any calls from people who distrust the vaccine. “Now, people are afraid to get vaccinated because they don’t want to miss a day of work because of side effects. It’s no fun carrying boxes all day in a warehouse if you’re tired and your arm hurts,” she says. The price to pay for an absence can be catastrophic.
« Si tu travailles pour une agence et qu: “If you work for an agency and you miss a day of work, they’ll replace you.” The IWC is currently in talks with employers and public health authorities to set up pop-up vaccination clinics at certain workplaces that would be open on Friday evenings so workers can recover over the weekend.
Pour plusieurs nouveaux arrivants et per: For many newcomers and people with precarious status, the idea of getting vaccinated to protect their loved ones from COVID-19 comes first. “We’re told, ‘Love one another,’ and getting vaccinated to protect yourself is in that spirit,” says Marie Mbodji, a recently arrived Congolese refugee who lives in Parc-Extension. She has already been vaccinated.
« C’est la seule façon de retourner à un: “It’s the only way to get back to a normal life,” adds Mamadou, who plans to get vaccinated as soon as possible. He can’t wait to see his friends again. Jill Hanley and Pénélope Boudreault hope the pandemic will bring Quebec closer to a truly universal health care system. “In the past year, we’ve seen a great openness to expanding the right to health care in Quebec,” notes Jill Hanley, who believes the trend needs to become widespread.
Si on donne accès aux soins à tout le mo: “If we give everyone access to care, without barriers and without fear, we won’t have to do all this work. The trust will already be there when the next crisis hits.”
